title: Geographic Center Finder: States and Countries
description: Look up the published geographic center of any US state or major country with the Geographic Center Finder — coordinates and nearest place. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the geographic center of the contiguous United States sits near Lebanon, Kansas — the fact behind a thousand roadside markers, and this page defaults to Kansas for a reason.
quick_answer: The Geographic Center Finder looks up the published geographic center of a US state or major country and gives its coordinates in decimal and degrees-minutes-seconds, a map pin, and the nearest named place. Search or pick the state or country — or enter two points and get their midpoint instead.

popular_table.note: A 'geographic center' depends on the method (balance point of the territory's shape, coastline treatment, islands included or not). Published centers carry their method with them; small differences between sources are method differences, not errors.

faq: What does 'geographic center' mean?

The balance point of the territory's area — imagine the state cut from cardboard and balanced on a pin. Coastlines, islands and projection choices nudge the result, which is why published centers are the ones worth quoting.
How accurate are the coordinates?
They are the published figures for each state or country, given as recorded. The nearest-place context helps you judge what visiting would involve.
Why is Kansas selected by default?
It holds the contiguous US center — the most asked-about middle in the country. A fitting default.
What is the two-point mode?
Enter any two points and get their geographic midpoint — unrelated to state centers, and the gateway to this site's halfway tools.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — centers are looked up, not located. Your position plays no part.
The center is in a lake or private land.
Common — balance points ignore ownership and water. The nearest named place is the visitable version of the pilgrimage.
Center of population instead?
A different, also published concept (where the average resident balances). This page is geographic area centers; the distinction is the lesson.
Countries beyond the US?
Major countries are included with their published centers where established. Smaller states' centers follow the same method caveats.
Historical centers?
Boundaries move, so centers do too — a state's 1900 center is a museum piece. The page carries current published figures.
Center of the Earth jokes aside — oceans?
Country centers can fall in water for archipelago nations; the published point is still the point, and the nearest named place is your dry-land answer.
Who publishes these centers?
National survey and mapping authorities (the USGS tradition in the US) and reference publishers. The page carries published figures rather than recomputing its own, stated in the method note.
